prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which interrogates large ensembles of atoms at the magic wavelength and has taken optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a discovery-and-invention case of the kind the mandate asks for. The magic-wavelength idea is a specific, original concept (Katori, 2001-2003) that was realised experimentally with strontium, and Ye's group then showed that it delivers fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 with thousands of atoms interrogated at once. The result has been reproduced by many independent laboratories with Sr and Yb, and clock-to-clock comparisons across institutes and over fibre links are the direct experimental verification. It opens doors: relativistic redshift at millimetre scales, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a redefinition of the second that is now operational rather than speculative. Six of eight members ranked it in their top three or better, from different subfields, which suggests the case does not depend on one member's specialty. The two-name configuration is clean and fits the rule that we must be sure we have identified the people who did the original work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision metrology can be read as the continuation of the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single ions, so the committee must show that a lattice clock is a distinct invention and not a better version of an existing one. There is also a priority question that I can only partly settle from memory: Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and others contributed to the first demonstrations and the accuracy frontier, and two names cannot represent everyone. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and some colleagues may want to wait for it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a new measurement technique that removes Doppler and recoil shifts, with a good moment in time and a natural two-person prize, but notes that the citation must handle the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree on the core assessment, and I think the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice as the invention, so that the distinction from comb and single-ion work is built into the wording. Where I would qualify his view is on the other contributors: I would not wave away Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley as lightly as he does. The committee should check the early strontium lattice papers (Takamoto and Katori, Ludlow and Ye, Lemonde's group) to confirm that Katori and Ye are the originators and the record-setters, respectively, before we settle on two names.

responses.point: Danielsson puts baryon acoustic oscillations first as a clean observation of nature that turned dark energy from an inference into a measured expansion history, with Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock as a defensible trio.
responses.response: I accept that BAO is a very important result and that it has been reproduced by several surveys, but I have a serious difficulty with the attribution. The 2005 detections come from two large survey collaborations, and as Danielsson himself says, the theory of the acoustic feature precedes the measurement (Peebles and Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich). Three named people cannot clearly represent the original experiment, and I am not absolutely sure that we would be crediting the people who did the work. The lattice clock has a sharper definition of who did what. I also note his concern about repeating the cosmology prizes of 2006, 2011 and 2019, which I share to some extent.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first, as a clear physical idea with quantitative theory and confirming experiments, and prefers the theory-led trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, while admitting he is working from memory.
responses.response: This is my strongest alternative, and I agree on the scientific weight. But I disagree with the trio: it credits the theory twice and the experiments once, and it leaves out the first 3D observation by ARPES, which I think matters for a prize on experimentally verified discoveries. That is why I put Hasan in my own configuration instead of Mele. He is right that the original Kane-Mele graphene phase is not realised in real graphene because the spin-orbit gap is too small, which makes the priority rest on the concept; I would want the committee to be explicit about that, and about the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that sits outside the credited names, before it settles on any names.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first as exact statements about work and entropy production in small systems, now routine in single-molecule experiments, with Jarzynski, Evans and Crooks as a coherent trio.
responses.response: The universality is attractive, but this is a theory-led candidate, and Mehlig himself notes that the experimental tests (RNA unfolding, colloids, trapped particles) were done by people who are not on the list. The Physics Prize is for a discovery or invention verified by experiment, and here the original experimental verification is not credited. The priority question with Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan and others is also unresolved. I would need a much clearer record before I could support it, and it did not make my own ballot.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven discovery that opened neutrino astronomy, and puts the lattice clock second, with Halzen and Karle as a fair two-person prize but with real attribution questions in a roughly 300-person collaboration.
responses.response: I sympathise with the instrument-centred argument, which is close to my own, and I ranked B046 myself. My reservation is about credit. The diffuse flux is solid, but source identification rests on a few objects, and I am not sure that two names capture who did the original work among AMANDA, DUMAND and IceCube. I think the lattice clock currently has the cleaner attribution and a more complete story. I would be glad to hear whether he can document the individual roles of Halzen and Karle in the discovery analysis, since that would change my view of B046.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and the trapped-ion proposal second, and he agrees that the lattice clock is natural as a two-person prize, while declaring that he works in superconducting circuits and that his judgment on that field should be discounted.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure. On the lattice clock we agree on the attribution. On circuit QED I have a qualification: it is a strong coupling-in-a-chip result with wide adoption, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits makes me reluctant to reward a further circuit candidate so soon, and Girvin and Devoret are not in the credited names, so the attribution is incomplete. I also think it is closer to a platform engineering success than a single discovery.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether Katori and Ye are indeed the right two names, given the early strontium work of Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and others, which I cannot verify from the provided files.
Whether to wait until the redefinition of the second has been decided.
The division of credit among 2D and 3D topological insulator work, which decides how strong B045 is as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted candidate. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names. My colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics and has declared his own interest in circuit QED and mechanical quantum systems; that is not a conflict for my preferred configuration, but I will weigh his arguments on B039 and B032 accordingly.
